Get the PicoGo AM52 for just $38.29 with code MACWORLD1. Enjoy ultra-slim portability, Qi2.2 fast wireless charging, strong magnetic attachment, and an optional built-in cable for effortless iPhone 17 charging.

Get The Deal




We put the best portable chargers through a series of rigorous iPhone recharging tests, and have listed the winners by power, portability and functionality:
Best high-capacity 10k MagSafe power banks
Best small portable 5K magnetic power banks
Best multi-device charging MagSafe power banks 
Best capacity magnetic power bank for you
You should consider size when it comes to a power bank: physical size and battery capacity. The higher the battery capacity, the more recharging power you’ll get from the power bank—but you’ll also be carrying around a larger, heavier item. Lighter, slimmer power banks are easier to pocket even when clamped to your phone. Larger power banks might not fit in your trouser pocket and can slide off easier when pocketed even if clamped magnetically.
10K power banks (with a 10000mAh battery capacity) can charge a phone close to two times over, while 5K (5000mAh) battery packs usually stretch between 60-75%, which is often enough to get you to the next wall-socket powering opportunity. If you are relying on the power bank for long-haul travel or a camping trip, a 10K battery or higher will suit you better. Belkin even offers a mid-range 8K power bank.
Milliamp hours (mAh) is quite a blunt measurement of battery capacity. It’s great for quickly differentiating between power bank sizes but we also list the capacity in the more accurate watt hours (Wh).
Wireless power bank charging speed
Wireless charging speeds vary from 7.5W (MagSafe Compatible) to 15W (certified MagSafe and Qi2), all the way to the very fastest wireless charging at 25W (Qi2.2). While it’s not as efficient as using a cable to charge a phone, magnetic wireless charging is a step closer to doing away with cables altogether. Qi2 25W brings wireless charging close to wired speed but only iPhones 16 and later support that speed, and some power banks include a built-in USB-C cable for even faster charging up to 45W. The iPhone Air can manage 20W max on even a 25W charger. See Which wireless tech is best for your iPhone?.
We have listed the speeds at which each portable power bank can be charged itself (Input charger) and charge the iPhone (Output charger). The higher the wattage, the faster the charging should be.
Best high-capacity 10K MagSafe power banks
A 10000mAh (10K) battery is the sweet spot for both power and portability. 5000mAh (5K) power banks reviewed further down are slimmer, lighter and easier to pocket, but generally offer a maximum of 70-80% recharge potential versus a 10K power bank that should be able to recharge an iPhone at least one and a half times over.

The Kuxiu S3 was the first semi-solid-state 25W magnetic wireless power bank to enter the Macworld Lab. A semi-solid state (SSS) power bank is more energy-dense than a traditional liquid electrolyte power bank because its semi-solid electrolyte is less prone to leakage and thermal runaway. SSS is therefore more durable, safer and offers more charge cycles so will last longer.
Indeed, not only does it tick those boxes but its also boasts three other top-end features: a built-in USB-C cable, integrated kickstand, and super-clear digital battery display.
Only the iPhones 16 and 17 support the very fastest wireless tech Qi2 25W, and only the iPhone 15 and later have a USB-C charging port. Older iPhones (from 12 on) can use a 25W charger such as the S3 but are pegged back at 15W—still faster than the 7.5W found on cheaper power banks.
Switch to wired charging via the integrated USB-C cable and you’ll achieve up to 35W so even faster.
The S3 has a 10000mAh (10K) battery capacity and managed to recharge that same iPhone to 177%—so up to 100% then another 77% when it came to a second recharging task. That’s not the top score we’ve had in our 10K power bank tests: the champ so far is the Ugreen MagFlow Air 10K, which scored an unmatched 208%, with the EcoFlow RAPID 10K and Anker MagGo Slim scoring 190% or close—both are reviewed here. But 177% is above average.
The same company offers two other 25W magnetic power banks: the similar S4 reviewed below, and the K1 Ultra (reviewed in our multi-device section below) that has a neat slide-out panel that can charge your Apple Watch or AirPods at the same time as the iPhone.

That might not sound a lot but when you’re in a rush to charge your phone, every minute counts. 25W wireless charging is limited to the iPhone 16 and 17 families, running at least iOS 26; older iPhones will charge at 15W using this power bank.
Most 10K wireless power banks are around 22mm deep, so the 16mm-thin Baseus PicoGo Magnetic 10K Power Bank (AM52) is one of the slimmest we’ve tested. The Kuxiu S4 reviewed above is even slimmer at just under 14mm but the AM52 is certainly thinner than most.
The AM52 is an output blazer is more ways than one. How we tested
MagSafe charger testing was conducted using an iPhone 13 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro and 16 Pro, subscribed to a 5G network and WiFi, with screen off and all default settings.
Our test is a simple battery recharge shootout. We let our test-unit iPhone Pro (3095mAh battery capacity) drain to just 10% and then set the Battery Pack to work recharging the phone. We then assigned the charger a score of whatever percentage it managed to charge the iPhone to and subtract the 10%; we test each model at least twice.
It’s not a real-world test of day-to-day use where you’ll likely be using your phone for various tasks (of varying battery usage) and in different environmental conditions and network configurations. But it does give us a common score format that we can use to compare different battery-pack models.

				
					

				
			
Why is magnetic wireless better?
The MagSafe connection to Apple’s iPhone is precise enough to make wireless charging more efficient as around 20% of non-magnetic power loss is from poor placement of a phone and the wireless charging pad. Standard Qi wireless charging can lose as much as 50% of the portable battery’s power, but MagSafe and Qi2 wireless charging loses ‘just’ 30%. Hot out of the gadget laboratory, the new Qi 2.2 (also known as Qi2 25W) brings even faster 25W wireless charging for the iPhone 16 and 17. 15% will be plenty fast enough for most of us but who doesn’t want the fastest possible charging when your iPhone’s battery icon is in the red?
Why comparing Watt Hours is better than Milliamp Hours
Phone batteries are generally rated in Milliamp Hours (mAh) but this is a measure of electrical charge, while a Watt Hour is equal to one watt of energy consumed for one hour of time.
When comparing battery capacities and how much a power pack will boost a phone’s internal battery, energy is more important than electrical charge.
And mAh ignores a battery voltage, which determines the wattage (power) of a battery.
If the mAh is the same, the higher the voltage, the greater the actual stored power.
For example, Apple’s MagSafe Battery Pack is rated at just 1460mAh but it has a higher voltage potential (7.62V) than the iPhone (3.81V) or other battery packs, meaning that it can provide more power to an iPhone than its mAh suggests; in fact, it is actually 2920mAh.
To go into further depth about this read our feature iPhone battery capacities compared that also lists all iPhones battery life in mAh and Wh.
Anatomy of a magnetic power bank

				
					

				
			
TORRAS




A lot more than a battery goes into the making of a magnetic power bank.
Of course, the battery is the most important component, but the wireless charging coils and magnetic connection are vital for efficient and therefore fast and powerful charging. The transmitter coil transfers power by electromagnetic induction.
The magnets need to be set up to exactly connect the transmitting coils—here on the power bank— to the receiving coils, in this case inside the iPhone.
The example shown above is the Torras MagStall Wireless Power Bank, reviewed in our chart. You can see the various parts, including that power bank’s rotating stand/handle.
Which magnetic wireless tech is right for each iPhone?
iPhone 7 and earlier: Don’t support wireless charging. 
iPhone 8 – iPhone X/XS/XR: Support wireless charging. iPhone 8 and later can charge wirelessly at 7.5W but on a less efficient non-magnetic Qi pad.
iPhone 11 and earlier: Don’t support MagSafe. iPhone 8 and later can charge wirelessly but on a less efficient non-magnetic Qi pad.
iPhone 12 – iPhone 15: Support MagSafe and Qi2. Can wirelessly charge at 7.5W with “MagSafe-Compatible” power banks and chargers, and at 15W with certified MagSafe or Qi2 power banks and chargers.
iPhone 16 – iPhone 17: Support MagSafe, Qi2 and Qi2.2. Can wirelessly charge at 7.5W with “MagSafe-Compatible” power banks and chargers, at 15W with certified MagSafe or Qi2 power banks and chargers, and at 25W with Qi2.2-certified power banks and chargers.
What about non-wireless power banks?
Wireless charging—especially magnetic wireless charging—is super convenient and does away with the need to carry around messy cables to connect your device to the battery pack.
But wired charging is nearly always faster and not much of an inconvenience if you are not out and about. Over on our sister site Tech Advisor I have reviewed the best power banks that includes standard non-wireless battery packs that might be a decent solution as well as the power banks reviewed above.
Do magnetic power banks work when the iPhone is in a case?
Yes, most quality iPhone cases are compatible with MagSafe having their own magnet ring to ensure a close connection between the power bank’s magnetic charging coils and the iPhone’s own. You can find exactly which are supported in our roundups of the best iPhone 17 cases, best iPhone 16 cases and best iPhone 15 cases.

title: Apple's Bid to Use Chinese Chipmaker as Leverage Backfires
content:
Apple's attempt to use Chinese memory maker CXMT as leverage against Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix has backfired, with the two Korean chipmakers ending up with more pricing power rather than less, DigiTimes reports, citing South Korean and Chinese trade press.


This year, Apple has explored CXMT and fellow Chinese chipmaker YMTC as potential DRAM suppliers, and had progressed to testing CXMT's chips as memory shortages pushed up the cost of almost all Apple devices. Apple hoped a credible Chinese alternative would pressure Samsung and SK Hynix into cutting their own prices, a tactic it has used before with OLED suppliers and contract manufacturers.

TechTimes, requires around 30% more wafer starts to produce the same output. That extra cost means matching Samsung and SK Hynix's prices is CXMT's floor, not a discount it's able to offer, so when Apple pushed for a lower LPDDR5X quote, CXMT turned it down and held pricing at or above the Korean suppliers' own rates.

Digital Daily reports that Chinese device makers Huawei and Xiaomi have already locked up most of CXMT's output through long-term, high-price contracts, so the company doesn't need Apple's business badly enough to negotiate.

title: OpenAI Asks Judge to Dismiss Apple's Trade Secrets Lawsuit
content:
OpenAI has asked a federal judge to dismiss Apple's lawsuit accusing the AI company of stealing trade secrets, calling the allegations "meritless."


Lawyers for OpenAI said Apple's suit twists the actions of its employees. Bloomberg reports that the filing defends Chief Hardware Officer Tang Yew Tan, who spent 24 years at Apple as VP of product design for iPhone and Apple Watch before leaving to co-found io Products with former Apple design chief Jony Ive. io merged with OpenAI in July 2025. OpenAI said Tan followed normal industry recruiting practices when interviewing Apple staff.

excerpts of text messages it says back up that account. "Apple should not be permitted to use a baseless and pretextual lawsuit," OpenAI's lawyers wrote.

OpenAI's motion argues Apple never properly identified what information actually counts as a protectable trade secret. The company said it has no interest in Apple's confidential material because it is "building something entirely new and different from anything at Apple."

Axios reported that OpenAI's filing also disputes how Apple built its case. According to OpenAI, Apple's own security practices, including letting staff use personal iCloud accounts for work and later reviewing personal messages left on company devices, are what gave former employees leftover system access in the first place, not evidence of a coordinated theft. The 31 page filing repeatedly frames the case as Apple trying to cover for its own struggles, with variations of the word "fail" appearing nearly 50 times.

OpenAI's filing also revisited an earlier dispute over how the two sides first fell out of contact. Apple's suit had claimed OpenAI never responded to its outreach in February, and that the two sides discussed the matter with OpenAI's general counsel. OpenAI says neither is true, and that the breakdown traced back to Apple's own outside counsel confusing two OpenAI employees with similar surnames and sending a message to the wrong person.

Apple filed against OpenAI in July, which accuses the company of running a scheme to pull confidential product information out of job candidates and new hires. Apple and OpenAI had spent about two years partnering to build ChatGPT integration into Siri, but the relationship soured as OpenAI moved into hardware, a shift accelerated by its acquisition of Ive's startup. Apple's suit claims more than 400 former Apple employees now work at OpenAI.

asking the same judge for a preliminary injunction to stop OpenAI from using any alleged trade secrets while the case continues, along with expedited discovery targeting Liu, Tan, OpenAI and its foundation, and io. Apple said its investigation has since turned up 11 more former employees who may have been witnesses or otherwise involved, beyond Liu, Tan, and previously named OpenAI employee Yu-Ting Peng.

Apple claims one former employee met with Liu and Peng before Peng's OpenAI interview and discussed proprietary information about unannounced products, and that another took screenshots of confidential documents relating to an unannounced Apple product before their own interview. Apple also said that after it filed its complaint, several former staffers now at OpenAI reached out about returning Apple issued devices they had kept.

title: Is the pro Mac dead?
content:
Macworld


After nearly 20 years, on a seemingly random Thursday, Apple finally pulled the plug on the Mac Pro. Apple later confirmed that it will no longer be selling its high-end Mac tower and has “no plans to offer future Mac Pro hardware.” The Mac Pro, once a symbol of Apple’s dominance in the PC workstation space, is well and truly dead.
Yes, yes, I know what you’re thinking: the Mac Studio exists and is aimed squarely at many of the same users that would have bought a Mac Pro. But while it matches or even exceeds the Mac Pro in processing power, the Mac Studio lacks the things that made the Mac Pro unique, namely the expansion and cooling capabilities of a tower computer. The Studio is a high-end performance machine, but not really a pro machine and more than a Mac mini with the same chip.
And with Apple releasing the MacBook Neo earlier this year, it might seem like the company is turning its attention towards the budget end of the market at the expense of its professional customers. Without a clear ultra-high-end option, Apple’s most discerning and demanding users will have to either opt for the non-modular Mac Studio or look outside Apple’s ecosystem.
Pro or no?
Let’s be honest, Apple’s pro users haven’t been particularly well-served by the Mac Pro for some time. The Mac Pro’s last update came in 2023 with the M2 Ultra chip, which has since been surpassed by the M3 Ultra – present in the Mac Studio but never in the Mac Pro. Performance was therefore superior in a more affordable Mac.
There were also memory and storage differences that were frankly embarrassing for the Mac Pro. While it peaked at 192GB of RAM and 8TB of storage, the Mac Studio surpassed that with 256GB of memory and 16TB of storage. You paid less and got more.

				
					

				
			
In the years leading up to its discontinuation, the Mac Pro looked more powerful than it actuall was.

Thiago Trevisan/Foundry




Put together, that meant the reasons to get a Mac Pro were ever dwindling. All you were really left with as a reason to cough up $6,999 or more was the ability to expand the internal storage and add some extra I/O. And few users could really rationalize that.
The fact that Apple updated the Mac Pro so infrequently, just three times in the last 14 years, tells you how low of a priority it was. The product almost certainly sold in such meager numbers as to make further revisions hard to support. This then fueled a vicious cycle: fewer people bought the Mac Pro due to its lack of updates, which then disincentivized Apple to continue working on it.
In the end, the Mac Pro was too niche to justify its continued existence. Apple had a choice to either continue developing it (with all the costs associated with that) or quietly kill it off. We shouldn’t be too surprised that it opted for the latter.
Shifting priorities
Of course, Apple’s high-end Mac offerings extend far beyond the Mac Pro. There are ample high-grade options around. So, where do true pro Mac users stand now that the Mac Pro is no more?
There’s not really a clear answer. For example, Apple refreshed its professional desktop monitor in March with the Studio Display XDR. Before the new model dropped, the Pro Display XDR was a true pro display, starting at $4,999 and offering specs that only the most demanding users needed. Despite its price, it was universally praised despite not having been updated since 2019. 
The 27-inch 5K model that replaced it is smaller and isn’t nearly as robust as its 32-inch 6K predecessor, but it’s a lot cheaper (starting at $2,899) and still has an array of high-end features, such as ProMotion and HDR. It’s a flagship display for sure, but not quite as pro as it was before.

				
					

				
			
The Studio Display XDR may be a technical downgrade from the Pro Display XDR, but it serves a wider audience.

Michael Simon / Foundry




Beyond that, the MacBook Pro is, of course, still going strong. It’s one of the most popular laptops in the world and certainly one of the strongest. Power users who need portable performance are incredibly well served by its Apple silicon chips, beautiful display, fantastic speakers, and incredible battery life. And there’s no sign that Apple is letting up there.
If you need power, Apple will insist that the Mac Studio and either the Studio Display or Studio Display XDR are what you need, but for some longtime Mac Pro users, the loss of a tower will mean Apple is giving up on an important segment of the market. But this is a textbook example of Apple skating to where the puck is going. Pro users are shifting, and Apple is adjusting its own lineup in response.
The rule of four
Dropping the Mac Pro should not be read as Apple scaling back its commitments to premium products. Rather, the company is merely adjusting its lineup to more closely reflect what its customers are actually interested in buying.
We’re not back to Steve Jobs’ famously concise product quadrant yet, but we’re getting closer. The idea of the quadrant was to fastidiously focus on desktops and laptops for professionals and consumers. In that order, we have the Mac Studio, the MacBook Pro, the Mac mini/iMac, and the MacBook Air/MacBook Neo.

				
					

				
			
The Mac Studio with an Ultra chip does a fine job replacing the Mac Pro at a more affordable price.

Petter Ahrnstedt




In a list like that, the Mac Pro was surplus to requirements. After all, when Jobs ditched a bunch of devices on his return to Apple in 1997, it wasn’t because he was giving up on those product categories. Rather, the products he cut simply weren’t good enough, and in many cases, the company returned in later years with better efforts.
Apple’s current pro-grade offerings still present an incredibly strong roster: There’s the Mac Studio, the MacBook Pro, and the Studio Display XDR, all products at the top of their game. That’s a hearty meal for any high-end user to dive into. But the days of ultra-high-end machines specced and priced for a specific group of users appear to be over.
Ultra is the new Pro
For a few years now, Apple has used the Ultra tag where the Pro signifier once sufficed. So far, we’ve gotten the Apple Watch Ultra, but rumors report Apple is planning to greatly expand that range later this year.
First up, there will be the iPhone Ultra. Although the name might sound new, you know this product: for years it’s been talked about as the foldable iPhone. A device as advanced as that, coupled with Apple’s famous premium trappings, would easily justify its spot at the top of the iPhone hierarchy and a price tag to match. There’s even the possibility of an “Ultra” upgrade for the AirPods, complete with cameras and sensors that could feed directly into Siri.
Of course, Apple’s non-Mac devices such as the iPhone and AirPods have always had a different definition of what “pro” means. But Ultra is coming to the Mac too. There’s the Mac Studio, which will soon get an M5 Ultra processor to make it the fastest Mac ever made. And the Ultra branding is expected to come to the MacBook, too, with the long-anticipated MacBook Pro with a touchscreen OLED panel. But is a touchscreen laptop really a pro machine? Do Apple’s highest-end users really want a touchscreen on their Mac, or would they rather have SSD slots and aftermarket graphics upgrades?
Apple’s Ultra lineup is certainly going to be a high-end tier, with expensive price tags and cutting-edge features that live up to their flagship branding. But where does that leave Apple’s pro users? If Apple is shifting the definition of “Pro” from extreme high-end niche products built for demanding users to high-priced products that showcase the latest design and breakthroughs, where does that leave pro Mac users? Because once everyone is a pro, then no one will be.

title: Meta's New Mac Coding Agent Costs Up to 20x Less If You Let Meta Train on Your Data
content:
Meta today launched Muse Code, a terminal coding agent available for macOS and Linux. Muse Code is in beta, and it is powered by Muse Spark 1.2, ‌Meta‌'s newest model.


‌Meta‌ CEO Mark Zuckerberg said Muse Code can accomplish complete software engineering tasks across large repos. It can plan out changes, write code, and validate results using multiple persistent subagents.

Muse Code is ‌Meta‌'s equivalent of OpenAI's Codex and Anthropic's Claude Code, and it is ‌Meta‌'s first major push into agentic coding.

There are several default skills available, such as /plan for turning a task into an approval-gated plan, /grill for stress testing a plan, and /goal for working toward the successful completion of an objective. Muse Code maintains an append-only local event log of every model call, tool run, approval, and edit, so it can resume where it stopped if it crashes.

Muse Code can be used through the Mac's terminal after a one-command install, and there is no dedicated app available. The model is priced at $1.25 for 1 million input tokens and $4.25 for 1 million output tokens, but ‌Meta‌ is offering a discount for users who give the company permission to use their prompts and completions to train future AI models.

With the Contributor tier enabled for ‌Meta‌ model training, Muse Spark 1.2 is priced at $0.10 for 1 million input tokens and $0.20 for 1 million output tokens. The Standard tier costs more and does not let ‌Meta‌ use prompts to train its models.

title: SpaceX Plans Starlink Mobile Service to Compete With Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile
content:
SpaceX shared plans to create a cellular service during its first earnings call after its IPO, reports Reuters. SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell said the company will "build out terrestrial" with the spectrum that it acquired from EchoStar.


She added that SpaceX intends to make Starlink a "true mobile service" that will win "quite a few" customers from Verizon, AT&T, and T-Mobile. Shotwell declined to discuss the costs involved in the endeavor and said SpaceX had "great and new ideas" on how to build a mobile service, such as a large number of lower-cost base stations paired with Starlink dishes instead of cell towers.

SpaceX agreed to pay $19.6 billion to acquire 65 MHz of wireless spectrum licenses from EchoStar in 2025. The spectrum will allow SpaceX to expand its direct-to-cell Starlink satellite service to include ground-based infrastructure.

Reuters that without an MVNO (Mobile Virtual Network Operator) agreement with a major carrier, it would be extremely difficult for Starlink to compete with AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile. 65 MHz is tiny compared to the spectrum owned by the big U.S. mobile operators, and they're unlikely to lease capacity to a competitor.

SpaceX plans to launch its next-generation Starlink Mobile satellites in 2027, and upgraded service that's "100 times better" than current direct-to-cell service is targeted for the end of that year. Shares of AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon fell 2 to 4 percent following the SpaceX earnings call.

title: Apple's iCloud Private Relay is Leaking Users' Real IP Addresses
content:
Apple's paid Safari protection feature that promises to keep your IP masked doesn't always work, according to security researchers Tommy Mysk and Talal Haj Bakry. It turns out iCloud Private Relay can expose your real IP to websites that use or pretend to use passkeys.


‌iCloud‌ Private Relay is a service included with paid ‌iCloud‌+ plans. It is supposed to hide your IP and DNS information when you browse the web using Safari, but it is not a VPN that masks all traffic from a device. Passkeys use the WebAuthn standard, which stores a private key on your device, not the Safari browser. The request the system sends to the website isn't protected by Private Relay and can leak your IP address.
WebKit hands WebAuthn ceremonies to the operating system's credential service, which issues the HTTPS request itself, directly from the device and unaware of any proxy the host app configured. A page can set rpId to a host of its choosing, and the fetch fires even without user interaction: with mediation: "conditional" and no UI ever appears. [...]


An attacker who wants to find someone's protected IP can do so by setting up a website that uses WebAuthn. There is no visible passkey prompt and no other indication that an IP address has been accessed in the background.

iOS 26) reveals a user's real DNS servers, while WebTransport (added in iOS 26.4) can reveal an IP address.

told 404 Media that it is investigating the report.

created a website to let you test whether Apple's service is leaking your IP address. Since the issue is baked into how WebKit works, some third-party browsers are affected too. Apple will need to address the issue, and in the meantime, users can opt for a VPN for more protection.

title: iCloud Private Relay might leak your IP address, even when you use Safari
content:
Macworld


A pair of security researchers found a critical problem with Apple’s iCloud Private Relay feature. Even when using Safari, a website can fairly easily get your real IP address.
Researchers Talal Haj Bakry and Tommy Mysk just disclosed the issue. Apple is aware of it; according to a report form 404 Media, Mysk said, “We have already informed them. They said the issue was ‘dire,’ but they let us disclose the issue. They didn’t provide any time when they will address this.”
Here’s how it works, in basic terms: iCloud Private Relay is a nice security feature but it is not a VPN. It only works when you use Safari. Passkeys—the helpful biometric alternative to remembering different passwords for every site—operate outside the browser, using the WebAuthn framework on Apple devices. So if you set up a website to make a request for a Passkey credential origin, it’s not protected by iCloud Private Relay because the Passkey request is technically happening outside the browser.
Of course, if you’re an everyday user, you don’t have any reason to know or suspect this. You’re using Safari, you have the paid iCloud+ Private Relay service turned on, you should be hidden, right?
The issue also affects browsers that use WebKit’s proxy relay, including some Tor browsers. The researchers built a proof-of-concept site you can use to check if you’re affected.
We don’t know when Apple is going to address the issue, but a vulnerability in Hide My Email that exposed real email addresses was fixed very quickly by Apple after the issue became public. That only required a back-end server fix, while this iCloud Private Relay issue might require a software update on devices. The fact that Apple let the researchers disclose the issue before the fix means Apple wants users to know about the problem and suggests it could take some time to fix.
iCloud Private Relay is not a VPN
This is a good time to remind everyone that iCloud Private Relay is not a VPN. A traditional VPN routes all the internet traffic for your entire device through other servers, sometimes providing other features as well at the core network level. iCloud Private Relay operates only in the Safari browser. It’s a nice perk of iCloud+, but not a full VPN substitute.
That difference is the root cause of this new issue. You can be browsing with Safari and a website can make a special kind of request that happens outside the usual browser stack—by design—and thus is not affected by iCloud Private Relay. Apple will obviously need to address this quickly.

title: Apple Vision Pro Speeds Up Surgery by Almost 20%
content:
Surgeons who wore an Apple Vision Pro as their primary display during a tear duct procedure finished operations 19% faster than surgeons using a traditional monitor, according to a peer-reviewed study by UC San Diego.


The study, published in the journal AJO International (via iPhone in Canada), looked at 32 endoscopic surgeries to clear blocked tear ducts. In half the cases, surgeons wore Vision Pro headsets that streamed the endoscopic video feed directly into their field of view instead of looking at a monitor across the room, letting them keep a natural forward-facing posture throughout.

Average operative time came in at 34.4 minutes with the Vision Pro, compared to 42.7 minutes with the traditional monitor. Every case in both groups succeeded with no complications, and all five surgeons involved said they preferred operating with the headset, reporting lower physical and mental workload.

title: When is Apple’s next event? Dates, rumors, and what to expect
content:
Macworld


Apple’s WWDC keynote may be long behind us now, but Apple’s event calendar for 2026 is far from finished. With iOS 27, macOS 27 Golden Gate, and the latest Apple Intelligence and Siri updates now unveiled, attention is turning to the company’s next big launch.
Apple rarely confirms event dates far in advance, and there’s no guarantee an event will take place within its usual window. That leaves Apple fans – and anyone considering a new Apple device – wondering when the next Apple event will happen and what might be announced.
Luckily, Apple’s annual schedule is predictable, giving us a good idea of when the next keynote will happen – and which products are likely to launch. Based on Apple’s long-established schedule and reliable rumours, we can make informed estimates about when the next keynote is likely and which products could headline it. 
From the iPhone 18 lineup and new Apple Watches to potential Mac and iPad updates, here’s everything we know about Apple’s next event and what you can expect to see. Read on for a closer look at all of the events Apple is expected to hold in 2026 and beyond, and what could launch.


When is Apple’s next event?
Beginning of September (expected)
Apple has not yet announced the date of its next event, although the company has asked Apple Store staff to apply for the ” Event Support Experience Program.” Employees enter a lottery for the opportunity to assist with an Apple event scheduled for the first half of September. 
Based on Apple’s typical event schedule, we expect the company’s next event to be the annual iPhone launch in September 2026.
Looking at Apple’s event history over the past several years, we predict the September event will take place during the week beginning September 7, with September 8 or 9 the most likely dates, although it could be pushed back to September 15. 
As in previous years, Apple is expected to livestream the event, allowing viewers around the world to watch the company unveil its latest products. One notable change this year is that the keynote is expected to be hosted by John Ternus, who is set to succeed Tim Cook as Apple’s CEO following Cook’s retirement



Apple event calendar 2026

TimescaleEvent themeDatesProducts

March Special Experience2-4 MarchLaunched: iPhone 17e, MacBooks Neo, Pro & Air, iPad Air
JuneWWDCJune 8Expected: iOS, macOS, other software, Mac updates, AI news
September[iPhone event]TBCExpected: iPhone 18, new Apple Watch
October or November[Late fall event]TBCPossible: Macs and iPads? 





Apple has held two events so far in 2026, although the first was not an event in the traditional sense. On March 4, the company invited select media to hands-on “experiences” in multiple locations. In the run-up to that date, Apple also launched several products via press release, including the iPhone 17e, M4 iPad Air, and MacBook Pro M5 Pro and M5 Max, M5 MacBook Air and the MacBook Neo.
The second event was WWDC, which began with a keynote on June 8. At the WWDC keynote Apple outlined the upcoming changes to its operating systems, including iOS 27 and macOS 27 Golden Gate.
Looking ahead to the fall, Apple is expected to unveil the iPhone 18 Pro, a foldable iPhone Ultra, and more at an Apple event in September.
A second, late-fall event in October or November is possible, though less certain and typically focused on Macs or iPads.

				
					

				
			
Here’s when the 2026 Apple events might take place.

Foundry





 FAQ 


1.
What will Apple announce at the next event?
Apple’s September event is the biggest and most watched Apple event of the year. It’s the venue at which Apple unveils the new iPhones and Apple Watches for the next year. 
We expect Apple to launch the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and Apple Watch Series 12 at a September event. Apple may also reveal the new folding iPhone, thought to be called the iPhone Ultra.
Rumors also point to a new and improved HomePod and Apple TV. The iPad and iPad mini are also overdue an update so may arrive at the same event.
We may also see updates to the Mac Studio and Mac mini.





2.
What time does the next Apple event start in U.S., U.K. and other global time zones
Apple keynotes usually start at 10 am PT. That translates to the following times in the countries where most of our readers live:
U.S.: 10 am PDT, 11 am MDT, 12 pm CDT, 1 pm EDT
Canada: as above, plus 2 pm ADT
U.K.: 6 pm
Europe: 7 pm CEST, 8 pm EEST
India: 10:30 pm IST
Australia: next day — 1 am AWST, 2:30 am ACST, 3 am AEST
New Zealand: next day — 5 am NZST
The timings are generally the same for all Apple Keynotes, but can be slightly different if Apple holds the event during the period of a couple of weeks when the clocks have changed in the U.S. but not elsewhere (in 2026 the clocks will change in the U.S. on November 1, while in the U.K. they change on October 25).
Sometimes Apple holds events at different times, for example, in October 2023 the event was held in late afternoon in San Francisco, which meant it was midnight in the U.K. 
If Apple doesn’t hold an event and instead just issues a press release that usually happens around 8 am PT, 11 am ET and 4 pm U.K. time.





3.
How long do Apple events usually last?
Apple keynotes usually last between one and two hours and feature CEO Tim Cook along with various other Apple executives – with Apple’s John Ternus, stepping into the CEO role in September 2026, it is likely we will see more of Ternus in future keynotes.
WWDC and the September event tend to be longer keynotes; the spring and late-fall events can be slightly shorter.
For example, the September 2024 event was 1 hour 38 minutes.





4.
How often does Apple hold events?
There can be as many as four Apple events in a year:  
Spring Event
WWDC in June
iPhone Event in September
Late Fall Event in October
This event calendar is by no means set in stone, though, with the spring and October events being less regular. Some years, Apple doesn’t hold a spring event at all. In 2025 Apple only held two events preferring instead to announce new products via press release.





5.
Does Apple take part in other events?
Apple doesn’t participate in big industry-wide events such as CES, IFA or E3. Instead Apple invites the press and industry professionals to Apple Park to hear all about its latest products and services. Apple calls these ‘events’ and it streams them live online to millions of viewers.





6.
Does Apple ever announce products without an event? 
Apple frequently announces products without a keynote event, often opting for press releases or multi-day announcement windows. In recent years, the company has increasingly reserved its large-scale media events for major flagship launches, such as the primary iPhone lineup in September, while using press releases for iterative updates or “chip bumps” that may not warrant a full hour-long presentation.





7.
How to watch an Apple event
Apple events are typically broadcast across several digital platforms, allowing viewers to tune in from almost any device. While the company previously restricted access to its own hardware or the Safari browser, these barriers have been removed in recent years.
You can access live Apple presentations through the following official channels:
YouTube: This is often considered the easiest way to watch. Apple streams its keynotes live on its official YouTube channel, which can be accessed via any web browser or the YouTube app on smartphones, tablets, and smart TVs .
Apple.com: The company hosts a dedicated “Events” page on its official website. For the best experience on a PC, it is recommended to use Microsoft Edge on Windows 10 or later .
Apple TV App: The stream is available within the Apple TV app on iPhone, iPad, Mac, and Apple TV hardware. Keynotes are usually listed in the app’s lineup a day or two before the event begins .
Apple Podcasts: Apple also showcases its events through the Podcasts app on Apple devices, where you can watch the video presentation
You may also like to tune in to our Live Blog which will provide minute-by-minute text updates and analysis as products are announced.
Following the end of the event, detailed breakdowns will also be available on the Macworld Podcast, which can be found on Spotify, Soundcloud, and Apple Podcasts. 








When is the iPhone 18 event and what will launch?

				
					

				
			
Apple




When is the iPhone event?
September 2026 (TBC)
Apple’s iPhone launch event has become a regular fixture in September (aside from 2020 event when it was delayed until October – and the early January launches). 
In recent years the event has been held on September 9, so we could see Apple make the unveiling in the week of September 7 in 2026, with the event perhaps taking place on September 8 or 9. 
What will Apple launch at the September 2026 event?
We can be pretty confident that at least one new iPhone will launch in late 2026, although there may be some changes to the line up: we may see the iPhone 18 Pro, Pro Max launch in September, but the iPhone 18 may be held back until the spring of 2027. There are also rumors of a folding iPhone – aka iPhone Ultra launching in September.
Alongside the new iPhone 18 Pro we may see new Apple Watches. In 2026 the Apple Watch Series 12 should get a chip update, since the Series 11 is using the same chip as the Series 10 did. The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is said to be getting a fingerprint scanner. 
Apple is also rumored to have some upgrades coming to the HomePod and Apple TV to better equip them for Siri AI. 
Find out more about the September iPhone event in our dedicated article.







Will Apple have a second fall event in 2026?

				
					

				
			
Apple




Will there be a late fall event in 2026
The last time Apple held a late fall event was October 30, 2023, and before that October 18, 2021. So a late fall event isn’t unprecedented, but it is uncommon. Right now there is no way of knowing if Apple will hold a late fall event in 2026, or indeed, if it ever will again. Usually this event is to launch consumer Macs, but in recent years Apple hasn’t felt the need to hold an event to do that. Nearer the time we will know if there are big things planned that might warrant an event. 
What will Apple launch at the late fall 2026 event?
Mac or iPad launches are the most likely reasons for an Apple event during this timeframe, but Apple has not felt the need to hold a dedicated Mac event since the “Scary Fast” presentation in 2023, when it introduced the M3, M3 Pro, and M3 Max chips alongside updated MacBook Pro models. There could still be Mac-related announcements this year, particularly if Apple has yet to refresh the Mac mini or Mac Studio. The rumored touchscreen MacBook Pro could also make an appearance.
The timing of any new Mac releases will likely depend on whether the supply chain has fully recovered from the component shortages that have affected the industry throughout the year. These shortages have also lead Apple to raise prices for iPads and Macs. 
As for iPads, a new iPad or iPad mini are long overdue, so an October event would be a likely venue for those launches, if they don’t arrive in September.
For more information about Apple’s late fall events read: Apple’s October Event: Date, time and what will launch.







Will Apple hold a spring event in 2027? 

				
					

				
			
Michael Simon / Foundry




Apple’s spring events have become increasingly unpredictable. The company has not held a traditional spring event since May 2024, although it did invite members of the media, including Macworld, to a “Special Apple Experience” in 2026. 
Rather than a keynote presentation, the March 4, 2026 gathering was a hands-on showcase that followed three days of product announcements, including the MacBook Neo, iPhone 17e, and M5 MacBook Air.
Will Apple take a similar approach to spring product launches in 2027? It’s certainly possible. The format appeared to work well, allowing each product announcement to receive its own media coverage rather than competing for attention during a single event. 
Apple is expected to Apple will release three iPhone models in spring 2027:
iPhone 18 (base model)
iPhone 18e
iPhone Air 2
Apple may also update the MacBook Air with an M6 processor in spring 2027. A report from early August 2026 notes that Apple is currently struggling with memory shortages that are impacting MacBook Air stock, and the M6 update is seen as a potential, though not guaranteed, fix for the supply issues.







When is WWDC 2027

				
					

				
			
Foundry




When is the WWDC keynote?
In 2026 the WWDC keynote was on Monday June 8. In 2025 it started on Monday June 9. We expect WWDC will start on Monday 7 June in 2027. 
WWDC generally runs from the Monday to Friday in the second week of June. 
What Apple could launch at WWDC
WWDC is Apple’s big developer event at which it reveals plans for the operating systems that run on Apple hardware.
In June 2027 we expect Apple to unveil details of the iOS 28, iPadOS 28, the new macOS 28, updates to watchOS, tvOS, HomePod software, and an update to Apple’s realityOS.
Apple sometimes announces new hardware at WWDC, usually the high end models targeted at power users, so we could see new Macs.
Following the keynote on the Monday, developer events and sessions will run throughout the week. You can read more about WWDC date, times and everything you need to know in a separate article.







What did Apple launch at past events
So far in 2026 Apple has held an ‘experience’, which rather than being an event in the traditional sense, was a chance for journalists to get a look at products Apple had launched in the days prior, including MacBook Neo and iPhone 17e. The company also hosted the WWDC keynote on June 8, at which it revealed it’s plans for Apple Intelligence and Siri in iOS 27, macOS 27 and the other operating systems. 
In 2025 Apple only held two events. The first was its Worldwide Developers Conference (WWDC) on June 9, at which it introduced the new features coming in the next version of its operating systems, and the second was the huge September 9 Apple Event where it launched new Apple Watches, new AirPods Pro and the new iPhones for 2025.
Apple doesn’t have to hold an event to launch new products though. Prior to WWDC, Apple launched a new iPhone 16e via press release on February 19, a new iPad and iPad Air via press release on March 4, and a new MacBook Air and Mac Studio on March 5. 
Apple then went on to launch a new M5 MacBook Pro and M5 iPad Pro in October. No event was held to mark these launches.
In 2024, Apple held three events: one on Tuesday, May 7, at which it launched new iPads; a keynote to kick off WWDC on June 10; and an event on September 9 at which Apple unveiled the new iPhone 16, Apple Watch Series 10 and the AirPods 4. In October 2024 there was no event, but Apple did announce new products (iMac, Mac mini and MacBook Pro) via press release.
In 2023 there were three events: WWDC in June, an iPhone event in September, and Apple’s second fall event on October 30 (or after midnight on October 31 if you weren’t in the U.S.).
In 2022 Apple held three events: a spring event on March 8, WWDC on June 6, and the iPhone 14 launch on September 7. In other years Apple has held four events though.

title: The world's RAM supply crisis is going to get worse before it gets better
content:
Shockwaves from the global RAM and SSD crisis continue to echo through home electronics pricing, and RAM manufacturers are reaping massive profits. A fix is coming, but it is a long time away and may not make any difference at all to consumers.


This is what it feels like buying RAM these days.
It's been a long time since RAM pricing at retail has been something that we've needed to keep an eye on. We still don't need to track sales on DIMM sticks, given how Apple sells and packages RAM on the chip. What you buy initially is what you will end with.

Apple AirPods Pro 3 are premium true wireless earbuds from Apple. Released in September 2025, they add heart-rate monitoring, foam-infused eartips, stronger ANC, improved sound, longer battery life and IP57 water resistance.
Why we like them
The AirPods Pro 3 refine an already excellent formula with noticeably better comfort, stronger noise cancellation, richer sound and longer battery life while keeping the same launch price. Heart-rate tracking is a useful bonus, making them an easy recommendation for most Apple users.
Who are they best for
They’re ideal for iPhone users wanting premium wireless earbuds with excellent noise cancellation, secure all-day comfort and seamless Apple ecosystem integration. They’re especially appealing for fitness enthusiasts who can benefit from the new built-in heart-rate monitoring.

More comfortable foam-infused eartips with five sizes

What is battery life like
Battery life increases to around eight hours with ANC enabled, while the case provides roughly 16 additional hours. A five-minute charge delivers about one hour of listening time.
How good is the ANC
Active Noise Cancellation is substantially improved, thanks to new microphones, redesigned eartips and computational enhancements. Apple claims twice the ANC of the previous generation, with noticeably better Transparency mode too.
Verdict
The AirPods Pro 3 aren’t a revolutionary upgrade, but they successfully improve almost every aspect of Apple’s best earbuds. While missing ANC and wireless charging limits their appeal for frequent travellers, they remain one of the best value options for Apple users wanting dependable everyday wireless earbuds.

				
		
How to choose earbud headphones
There are a few factors to consider before you hit that buy button.
Type
Earbuds, or in-ear headphones, typically fall into three main categories:
Earbuds – the type of headphones included with every iPhone and iPod and sit loosely in your outer ears. Although earbuds don’t produce outstanding sound, they’re compact and relatively inexpensive. Apple’s stock ‘buds are actually decent as earbuds go; you’re not going to get a huge upgrade in sound quality by simply replacing them with a different model. Still, there are a few alternatives out there that provide modest improvements if you’re looking for a new set. Recommendations:
In-Ear-Canal Headphones: These headphones, also known as canalphones, use silicone or foam eartips that fit snugly—and fairly deep—in your ear canals. Like earplugs, they block most external noise, so they’re great for travel and noisy environments. They’re also capable of producing stunning audio quality. On the other hand, some people find canalphones to be uncomfortable, and the best ones come with an equally stunning price tag. If you decide to spend the big bucks on a set of high-end canalphones, we enthusiastically recommend going all-in and getting custom eartips—tips custom-made for your particular ears. The process requires an audiologist visit to get impressions taken of your ears, but the benefits include substantially better comfort. (On some models, you may gain better noise isolation and better sound quality, as well.) A step above custom eartips are custom in-ear monitors, which place the actual headphone circuitry in larger, custom-made earpieces.
Canalbuds: Canalbuds, which occupy a middle ground between earbuds and in-ear-canal models, have become quite popular. Compared to canalphones, canalbuds generally use smaller eartips that sit just inside the ends of your ear canals instead of deep inside them. Good canalbuds easily best earbuds in terms of audio performance and noise isolation, but fall short of good canalphones in those areas. On the other hand, canalbuds tend to be more comfortable than true canalphones because they don’t sit so deep and don’t fit so tightly; they’re also usually less expensive. (See our in-ear-canal-headphone primer, linked above, for more information on canalbuds.)
Battery life
This is crucial as many in-ear headphones have tiny batteries that help to keep the weight down but may only last for a few hours. That might be fine if you just want to listen to some music while you’re working out, but won’t be much use on a long journey by train or plane.
However, some in-ear headphones, such as Apple’s AirPods, also include a charging case that can top up the battery, so that’s something you should check on before buying any in-ear headphones.
Noise canceling
Some headphones are specifically designed for people who travel a lot or use headphones in noisy conditions and provide active noise-canceling (ANC) option that helps to block out background noise on trains and planes – although this can add quite a lot to the overall price of the headphones.
Note this isn’t to be confused with passive noise isolation (or often referred to as canceling), which is just the way physically having headphones in/on blocks sound – like putting earplugs or ear defenders on.
Sound quality
We’d always recommend trying out any new headphones in a store or showroom whenever possible, but we realise that’s not always practical or hygenic.
Compatibility
Most wireless headphones support Apple’s preferred AAC Bluetooth codec, ensuring good compatibility with iPhones, iPads and Macs. Many also support additional codecs such as aptX Adaptive, aptX Lossless, LDAC or LC3/LE Audio, which can deliver higher bit rates, lower latency or improved efficiency when paired with compatible Android phones and other devices.
Apple devices have never supported Qualcomm’s aptX family of codecs, instead relying on AAC for Bluetooth audio. While this has often been attributed to Apple’s preference for controlling its own audio ecosystem, it also means Apple users can’t take advantage of newer Qualcomm codecs such as aptX Adaptive or aptX Lossless when using third-party headphones.
That isn’t necessarily the drawback it once was. AAC remains a very capable codec, and Apple’s implementation is widely regarded as one of the best, delivering consistent sound quality and excellent battery efficiency. However, Android users with compatible devices may be able to enjoy higher-resolution or lower-latency wireless audio through codecs such as LDAC or aptX Lossless.
For Apple users, the most important thing is that headphones support AAC, as this provides the best wireless experience across iPhone, iPad, Mac and Apple Watch. If a pair also supports codecs such as aptX Adaptive or LDAC, that’s a useful bonus if you also own Android devices or other compatible hardware.
There are a few exceptions. Some premium headphones and earbuds, such as the Bowers & Wilkins Pi8, include a smart charging case that can act as a wireless audio transmitter. By connecting the case directly to a USB-C or 3.5mm audio source, it can stream audio to the earbuds using aptX Adaptive, bypassing the Bluetooth limitations of the source device and potentially improving sound quality and reducing latency.
It’s also worth noting that all of the Bluetooth headphones featured here work with Apple Watch, making them ideal for workouts, runs and listening on the go.

title: Are Apple’s live events returning for the iPhone Ultra launch?
content:
Macworld


As we count the weeks until the iPhone event, a Bloomberg report from Mark Gurman caused a bit of a stir this week. It wasn’t about features, design, or pricing—rather, it was about staffing at the September event.
According to a memo seen by Bloomberg News, Apple has instituted a lottery to give retail workers “the opportunity to participate in the Event Support Experience Program.” According to the memo, the event will take place the first two weeks of September, and winners will be selected by Aug. 17, per the memo. Winning employees will help “organize lines, check in guests, greet attendees, offer directions and support the security teams.”
Gurman says that Apple has long used retail employees for events like these, but I can’t remember a report like this previously. I searched for anything about a lottery or staffing opportunity and couldn’t find anything about a similar program in prior years. So opening the opportunity to head to Apple Park to all U.S. workers appears to be a new thing. 
Here’s where the plot thickens, so to speak. In a post on X promoting the story, Gurman wrote, “NEW: Apple gears up for in-person iPhone event in the first half of September, asking retail employees to apply for a lottery to work the event.” The story he links to doesn’t mention anything about an “in-person” event, but obviously the employees will need to be on-site to work the event.
The use of the phrase “in-person” is a loaded one. Apple hasn’t held a live keynote since September 2019 when it unveiled the iPhone 11 and Apple Watch Series 5. Since then, it has presented prerecorded online keynote presentations, sometimes inviting members of the press to watch at Apple Park.
However, there are signs that Apple could be returning. Back in March, Apple unveiled the MacBook Neo at events around the world to small crowds. It wasn’t anything resembling a full keynote, but at the New York event, incoming CEO John Ternus (then VP of Hardware) was on hand to introduce the new machine and lead attendees to the hands-on area. And he just happens to be taking over as CEO on September 1, mere days before the iPhone event.
If there was going to be a perfect time when Apple would return to in-person events, it’s this now. Not only is it John Ternus’ first event as CEO, but it’s also widely expected that Apple will introduce its first folding phone at the event as well. That easily makes it one of the most anticipated events of the past decade, so what better time to gather people for an old-fashioned live keynote?
Whatever the format, Apple will likely hold its iPhone event on Wednesday, September 9, or Tuesday, September 15. Along with the folding iPhone, Apple is also expected to release the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, and possibly Apple TV 4K and HomePod mini refreshes.

What is it? A modular 10K power bank that splits into two separate 5K battery packs with built-in USB-C connectors.
Who is it for? iPhone 15 or later owners who desire the flexibility of shareable power banks.
Who shouldn’t buy it? Owners of the iPhone 14 and older, or those looking for a magnetic power bank to wirelessly clamp to the back of their device. Instead, they should look to the best magnetic wireless portable chargers.
The Nimble SharePower isn’t magnetic in a charging capacity, so won’t clamp onto the back of your iPhone to immediately begin charging, but it is clever in another way: it’s a sharable battery that will serve not just you but a very grateful friend, colleague or trustworthy stranger.
SharePower is a 10,000mAh portable charger with a difference. Unlike a typical 10,000mAh power bank, the Nimble SharePower splits into two completely independent 5,000mAh chargers that can be shared between two people. Each half has its own built-in USB-C connection and extra USB-C port, allowing up to four devices to be charged simultaneously when separated. It’s a genuinely useful twist on the standard portable charger, making it ideal for iPhone 15 and newer users who regularly share power with friends, family or colleagues without being tethered together by a charging cable.
Magnetically modular
Together the SharePower measures 3.1 x 2.8 x 1 inch (78 x 70 x 25mm) and weighs 7.6oz (216g). Divided, the two parts are roughly equal, with the cabled module being the slightly larger.
The two parts come together magnetically and won’t fall apart without a meaningful effort.

				
					

				
			Magnetically together in Stack Mode, divided into two modules, and showing the integrated USB-C connectors inside.
Nimble




The section with the built-in 29.5-inch (75mm) USB-C cable has a standard four-dot battery capacity display, while the other—featuring an integrated flip-up USB-C connector—features a TFT LCD digital display showing the actual percentage remaining.
The cable also works as a handy carry loop.
How much charge does it actually provide?
Many 10K power banks are made up of two 5K cells. Nimble has just separated them more cleanly so they can work independently.
In Macworld’s famous real-world recharging tests we used one of the modules to recharge an iPhone 16 Pro from 0% to 87% before the power bank half section ran dry. That’s not far off the highest 5K score we’ve recorded (90%), from the Ugreen MagFlow Air 5K. As the Ugreen is a wireless charger, some of its power would have been lost due to wireless charging’s inherent inefficiency, and so the SharePower’s test score is maybe as high as it is die to the stronger wired connection (we used the built-in cable).
If both SharePower modules perform the same, that’s a high 175% score combined, which should keep two iPhones charged for at least another day’s use.
Which iPhones does SharePower work with?
The fact that both battery sections have built-in USB-C connectors means it’s good only for iPhones 15 and later. iPhone of an older vintage (14 and earlier) use Apple’s old Lightning connector and so aren’t supported using the two integrated USB-C connectors. Time to buy a new phone or one of the best magnetic wireless power banks. Alternatively you could connect to an older iPhone with a USB-C to Lightning cable—indeed in our tests we had two USB-C iPhones, a USB-C-cabled Apple Watch charger, and a USB-C to Lightning cable for our ageing AirPods case.
Don’t restrict this charger to just your iPhone. It can just as well charge your USB-C iPad, and as mentioned earlier, even a MacBook if you can leave it untouched during charging.
Will it charge faster than wireless?
Wired charging is always faster than wireless as it’s more efficient, with less power wasted in the connection between the charger and the phone’s coils.
You don’t have to divide SharePower into its two halves. You can use it stacked with a possible 35W USB-C PD total output to charge three devices: one via the short integrated USB-C cable, and two more via the side USB-C ports—20W USB-C PD per module when split in Share Mode.
When used as one unit—Stack Mode—it can charge at 35W PD, which is just about enough to keep a MacBook Air or small Pro going, and certainly fine for a MacBook Neo.
Wireless charging has a maximum of 25W, but that’s difficult to maintain due to the heat produced at such an output via wireless. Charger makers introduce fans to cool the devices down to reduce the chance of the phone throttling the power in order to stay safely cool. You don’t get as much chance of that with wired charging so charging speed stays faster for longer.

				
					

				
			
Nimble




How many devices can SharePower charge at the same time?
Each half of the Nimble SharePower has one of the USB-C ports for a second device, so separated you can charge four drives in total.
Section one has the USB-C cable and a USB-C port. Section two has the flip-up USB-C connector and a USB-C port. It’s simple therefore when split to charge two iPhones plus, say, an Apple Watch and your AirPods case at the same time.
In joined Stack Mode, three devices can be charged simultaneously as the foldaway USB-C connector is hidden when the two halves are magnetically joined.
Both halves can be recharged themselves at the same time as they join up with tiny pogo pins.
If you want a magnetic wireless portable charger to share, you could opt for a power bank such as the Kuxiu S3 that boasts a 25W magnetic wireless iPhone charging pad, a built-in USB-C cable, and a spare USB-C port. Its three device-charging prowess is one behind that of the SharePower when split and requires all the charging devices to be attached to the one unit, where the SharePower physically divides into two parts.
Wireless charging is neater than the split SharePower’s wired charging, but when sharing between people Nimble’s approach is much more convenient.

				
					

				
			Sharing is caring, but remember to politely ask for the module back before you part ways.
Nimble




Sharing caveat
Of course, you must remember to ask for the shared half to be returned or suddenly the Nimble SharePower becomes the once-shared power. This is where your generosity in the airport Departures lounge might come back to haunt you.
How much does the Nimble SharePower cost?
You can buy the Nimble SharePower at Apple and Apple UK or direct from Nimble. It costs $79.95 or £59.95.
It is available in three colors: white, pink, or blue. If you get excited, buy two of different colors, and mix and match.
Should you buy the Nimble SharePower?
The Nimble SharePower operates as one stacked 10K portable charger or two divided 5K battery packs. It’s a neat idea, well done—letting you share a power bank without being tethered to your desperately unpowered friend by a cable when charging your own iPhone at the same time.

title: Foldable Smartphone Sales to Rise 20% This Year Due to 'iPhone Ultra'
content:
Global foldable smartphone shipments are expected to grow 20% in 2026 compared to last year, with Apple's first entry into the category cited as one of the factors driving the increase, according to industry sources cited by DigiTimes.


The report notes that the broader smartphone market is contending with tighter supply of upstream logic chips and higher memory prices, but says the foldable segment is expected to keep expanding regardless. Samsung is expected to retain its lead in the category, while Apple, Huawei, and other brands are described as helping to drive growth, with the fourth quarter of 2026 flagged as the year's most important sales period.

Industry sources told the publication that wider foldable designs and Apple's move into foldables are giving the category a further lift. Nearly eight years of product development, along with a growing number of brand launches and a broader range of devices for buyers, have made foldables more mature and given manufacturers added momentum to expand shipments.

iPhone 18 Pro models this September, and has reportedly told suppliers to prepare to build around 10 million units this year. Supply chain analyst Ming-Chi Kuo has suggested the device may not be available to pre-order until the fourth quarter of 2026, a timeline that lines up with DigiTimes' framing of that quarter as the category's key growth window.

‌DigiTimes‌ added that that most consumers already expect device prices to rise, so demand should hold up as long as increases stay reasonable.

P64 better for 16-inch MacBook Pro
Our Verdict 
We loved the diminutive Iniu P62 that offered a 20K battery in the smallest possible form, and cooed over the 140W/25K P64. Now the 100W/25K P63 looks like the sweet spot between compact size and recharging power both in terms of capacity and output.

What it is: A high-capacity portable charger in a unique compact form.
Who is it best for? MacBook owners with the need to recharge their devices on the move.
Who shouldn’t buy it? 16-inch MacBook Pro owners are better served by the 140W PD P64 power bank.
Even magnetic wireless power banks are starting to look ordinary these days, and—as shiny as pillar-shaped laptop power banks can be—it’s difficult to get too excited about one on looks alone.
Power purists will scoff and tell me off for judging a power bank on anything other than milliamp hours and total wattage output, but as a Mac user I do reserve some aesthetic disposition.
In among the best laptop power banks we’ve tested are a selection from Iniu, which dares to be different and serves up some portable chargers that are as cute as they are powerful.
How the Iniu P63 compares with the P62 and P64
We have already reviewed two of Iniu’s power banks, this review looks at the third in comparison.  
P62: Best for MacBook Air owners and anyone who wants the smallest, most affordable laptop power bank. (See our review of the P62)
P63: Best for 13- and 15-inch MacBook Air and 14-inch MacBook Pro owners, and a great choice for 16-inch Pro users who don’t need maximum charging speed.
P64: Best for 16-inch MacBook Pro owners who want full-speed 140W USB-C PD 3.1 fast charging. (See our review of the P64)
The 20000mAh Iniu P62 can be bought in a stunning orange version, while the 25000mAh P64 is available in standout white and red colorways. Iniu clearly doesn’t carry over its unique design skills into its product-naming process.
The only downside to the 20K P62 is its maximum 65W total power output. It has three ports, a removable USB-C cable, and enough power to keep a medium-sized MacBook going all day. In our recharge tests the P62 repowered a 14-inch MacBook Pro from 0% to 87%. The P64 on the other hand can output the full 140W that a 16-inch MacBook Pro requires for Apple-certified fast-charging (PD 3.1). Its 25K battery pack scored 119% in our real-world tests.
There’s a middle-ground Iniu laptop power bank that’s as cute as the P62 and nearly as powerful as the P64. You won’t be surprised to know that Iniu calls it the P63.

				
					

				
			From left to right: Iniu P64, P62, P63,
Simon Jary




Iniu Power bank specs compared
Iniu P62
Battery capacity: 20000mAh (65Wh)
Fastest Power Output: 65W
Total Power Output: 65W
Power Input: 45W
USB ports: 1x USB-C (65W PD 3.0); 1x USB-C (35W); 1x USB-A (18W).
Dimensions: 4.3 x 2.8 x 1.1 inches (110 x 71 x 29mm)
Weight: 11.4oz (324g)
Macworld Test Score: 87%
Iniu P63
Battery capacity: 25000mAh (90Wh)
Fastest Power Output: 100W
Total Power Output: 110W
Power Input: 65W
USB ports: 1x USB-C (100W PD 3.0); 1x USB-C (45W); 1x USB-A (18W).
Dimensions: 4.3 x 2.7 x 1.4 inches (110 x 70 x 36mm)
Weight: 13.8oz (392g)
Macworld Test Score: 109%
Iniu P64
Battery capacity: 25000mAh (92.5Wh)
Fastest Power Output: 140W
Total Power Output: 145W
Power Input: 80W
USB ports: 1x USB-C (140W PD 3.1); 1x USB-C (45W); 1x USB-A (18W).
Dimensions: 6.3 x 3.2 x 1 inches (159 x 81 x 25mm)
Weight: 17.5oz (496g)
Macworld Test Score: 119%
In our real-world testing, the Iniu P63 achieved a Macworld Test Score of 109%, delivering substantially more usable power than the P62’s 87% thanks to its larger 25K battery and higher efficiency. While it doesn’t quite match the P64’s 119% score, it comes surprisingly close despite costing less and being considerably smaller and lighter. In practical terms, that means the P63 offers enough power to comfortably recharge every MacBook model on the go, making it an excellent all-round performer unless you specifically need the P64’s faster 140W charging for a 16-inch MacBook Pro.
The Iniu P62 is the best choice if your priorities are the smallest size and lowest price, making it ideal for lighter MacBook users. The P63 is the sweet spot of the range, combining a larger 25K battery, faster 100W charging and only a modest increase in size, giving it the best balance of portability, capacity and value. The P64 is the premium option, worth paying extra for only if you specifically need 140W USB-C PD 3.1 charging to fast-charge a 16-inch MacBook Pro at its maximum supported speed.
Which power bank has the highest capacity?
25000mAh power banks such as the Iniu P63 and P64 are at the high end of the portable charger capacity scale. Manufacturers are keen to keep the rated watt-hour (Wh) below 100Wh as that is the maximum allowed on board a plane, even in your hand luggage.
Ratings in milliamp hours (mAh) are fine to compare power banks at a glance, but the Wh rating is more important, and accurate. Both the P63 and P64 are labelled 25000mAh power banks but the P64’s 92.5Wh capacity is marginally more than the P63’s 90Wh.
The highest we’ve seen is 99.9Wh from the ReelCharge ReelPro and Sandberg Survivor, both labelled as 27000mAh. Anything with a battery capacity over 100Wh, we have reviewed in our tests of the best portable power stations.
Our real-world tests bear this out. The P64 scored a little higher (8% in relative terms) than the P63 despite both being labelled as 25000mAh.

				
					

				
			
Simon Jary




Which is the smallest laptop power bank?
You could charge a MacBook using any PD (Power Delivery) power bank, even one meant for an iPhone Air. However, we class a laptop power bank as one of at least 20000mAh.
At 4.3 x 2.8 x 1.1 inches (110 x 71 x 29mm) the Iniu P62 is the smallest laptop power bank we have tested. However, the P63 really isn’t that much bigger despite its 38% larger battery capacity. It measures 4.3 x 2.7 x 1.4 inches (110 x 70 x 36mm), so it’s a little deeper but otherwise the same.
Iniu claims that this size reduction is made possible by use of a high-density TinyCell and innovative HyperStack circuit technology, but every premium power bank manufacturer claims its technology is the smallest and safest. In the case of making a small power bank, Iniu’s claim can be taken at face value.
Which power bank is best for each MacBook?
Starting with the MacBook Neo, its required 20W PD makes it happy to work with any power bank. In its case, even a 10K power bank might suffice for its smaller (36.5Wh) battery capacity but the P62 is ample.
The 13-inch MacBook Air has a battery capacity of around 52WH and the 15-inch Air is 66.5Wh. 14-inch MacBook Pro batteries are around 72Wh and the 16-inch is 99.6Wh—any higher and you might not be permitted to take it with you on a flight.
If you do own a 16-inch MacBook Pro, the P64 is your choice as it boasts the 140W power output that laptop demands to charge the fastest.
While the P63 suits the MacBook Air, 14-inch MacBook Pro owners should look to the P63. That power bank is also fine for the 16-inch if you don’t mind the slower charging speed.
Want to know the exact battery capacity of your laptop? Read our MacBook battery capacities compared list.

				
					

				
			
INIU




Scoring high on the cute-o-meter
Iniu’s P-series power banks have a more compact, curvaceous shape than most laptop power banks, eschewing the standard pillar shape.
The company also offers a range of colors to choose from, differing from the regulation gray/silver tone seen everywhere else.
P62: Black, Metallic Silver, Metallic Coffee, Metallic Black
P63: Black, Metallic Silver, Metallic Coffee, Metallic Black, Red and Yellow.
P64: Black, White
We had seen the P62 in blue, red, orange, yellow and white colors, so you might need to buy now if you want the brightest colors. Also check the listings on Amazon, where you might find extra colors.

				
					

				
			
INIU




Which ports are found on the power banks?
If all you want to charge is your MacBook, a USB-C port is what’s required. But most high-capacity power banks offer a set, including extra USB-C and a legacy USB-A port, and some include one or more integrated cables. The Ugreen Nexode Pro Laptop Power Bank (25K) has two built-in cables.
P62: 65W USB-C, 36W USB-C, 18W USB-A
P63: 100W USB-C, 45W USB-C, 18W USB-A
P64: 140W USB-C, 45W USB-C, 18W USB-A
110W output is possible, using the P63’s two USB-C ports together at 65W+45W. But note that, as with most power banks, total power output dips when using more than two ports. In the case of the P63, the first USB-C port can handle 65W while 15W is shared by the other two ports. 
Both the smaller power banks ship with a detachable 100W USB-C GoCord Cable, while the P64 comes with a non-attachable 240W USB-C to USB-C cable.

				
					

				
			
Simon Jary




How much does the Iniu P63 power bank cost?
The mid-range Iniu P63 power bank is priced at $69.99 / £66.99 at Amazon but is sometimes cheaper direct from Iniu. This is an affordable price for such a high-capacity power bank.
In comparison, the P62 costs $50.99 / £58.99, and the P64 $94.99 / £89.99. Check the links as discounts are frequent.
Should you buy the Iniu P63 power bank?
The Iniu P63 hits the sweet spot in the company’s laptop power bank lineup. It packs a generous 25K battery and fast 100W charging into a remarkably compact design that’s only slightly larger than the 20K P62, while costing significantly less than the 140W P64. Unless you own a 16-inch MacBook Pro and need Apple’s fastest charging speeds, the P63 delivers the best balance of size, capacity, performance and value.
