title: Telegram Briefly Removed From App Store
content:
Apple briefly removed Telegram from the App Store on Monday night after a review found content that violated its guidelines against child sexual abuse material (CSAM), but restored the app a short while later, according to Reuters.


Reports of the removal began circulating around 9:30 p.m. ET on Monday, with searches for Telegram on the ‌App Store‌ returning nothing and the app's direct listing showing a "page can't be found" error. Existing users were not affected and could keep using the app throughout, and Telegram remained available on the Mac App Store. The app returned to the ‌App Store‌ roughly 40 minutes later, around 10:10 p.m. ET. Apple confirmed the reason for the takedown in a statement:

We briefly removed Telegram from the App Store after our review found content that violates our strict guidelines prohibiting child sexual abuse material. The app was subsequently restored after the developer promptly removed the content and banned the user who posted it.


Telegram said the action stemmed from a single account. "Apple reported one user sharing CSAM, who was immediately banned," the company said, adding that it has removed more than 337,900 groups and channels related to CSAM in 2026, on top of 29,640 removals in 2025 following reports from groups including the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children.


reports of my demise are greatly exaggerated 🍎
— Telegram Messenger (@telegram) August 4, 2026
 


Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, a longtime critic of ‌App Store‌ policy amid his own antitrust fight with Apple, argued on X that the takedown showed the need for more competition in app distribution. "Apple's ‌App Store‌ desperately needs competition worldwide," Sweeney wrote. "Apple capriciously removes a vital communication and privacy tool from availability to a billion users, and sadly this is business as usual." He went on to question the consistency of the standard Apple applied, noting the company "did not elaborate on how, if that is the standard for app removal, any communications app could operate at scale, including iMessage."

What are they? Foldable 3-in-1 travel chargers for Apple iPhone, Watch and AirPods.
Which one is best? The Gen 4 Roam is the newest and fastest, offering 25W Qi2.2 charging for iPhone 16 models. The Gen 1 delivers the best value at around $39, while the colourful Gen 3 Orange/Teal and Gen 2 Cherry Blossom editions are the best picks for style.
Who shouldn’t buy it? If you aren’t travelling with all your Apple gear, check out instead the more fixed best wireless iPhone chargers and best Apple Watch chargers we’ve tested.
We recently reviewed the clever and rather lovely Mophie Roam 3-in-1, but while researching it we came across a bunch of other Mophie travel chargers that are still on sale and certainly caught our eye. 
Mophie continues to sell all four generations of its 3-in-1 travel chargers, making it easy to get confused by the different designs, colours, charging speeds and prices. 
In this guide we’ll compare every model to explain the differences and help you decide which best suits your needs, whether you prioritise the latest technology, fastest charging, best value or a distinctive limited-edition colour.


How do the Mophie travel chargers compare?
Mophie has a neat don’t-look-at-me black 3-in-1 travel charger for iPhone, Watch and AirPods case that folds up into small wallet form that fits into a cute case. At the time of writing, you can find it reasonably priced at under $40 or a little more on Amazon.
But it’s hard not to fall in love with a couple of limited-edition versions with colors (and much higher prices) that will make you sit up and notice. There’s a fun, postmodern orange and teal limited edition Mophie 3-in-1 travel charger that we’ve reviewed here and is guaranteed to brighten up your day when powering up your Apple devices. And there’s a slightly older Cherry Blossom pretty pink model that’s super cute.
The latest model is the Roam that is built on Mophie’s clever StealthCharge technology that maximizes 25W iPhone charging speeds for iPhones 16 and later. Read our Mophie StealthCharge Roam 3-in-1 Travel Charger review. The Roam is a great travel charger, but you should also consider previous-generation models for some fun colors and cheaper prices.
All these 3-in-1 chargers work with any iPhone (12 or later), any Apple Watch model, and AirPods with a wireless-compatible case.

				
					

				
			The Mophie 3 in 1 Travel Charger from the side. 
Simon Jary



				





Best Overall: Gen 4 Design Roam (2026) – Qi2.2 certified with StealthCharge
The newest model is the Gen 4 Mophie Roam (2026), introducing Qi2.2 with StealthCharge technology, a redesigned bi-fold design, improved thermal architecture with passive cooling to help sustain the fastest 25W wireless charging for iPhone 16 and newer models, and a redesigned, more water-resistant travel case. If charging speed is your priority, the Roam is the clear winner, thanks to its enhanced thermal design that maintains faster charging than the older 15W models.

Best Value: Gen 1 Design (2021)
For the best value, the Gen 1 (2021) stands out, often selling for around $39, making it a bargain if you don’t need the latest charging speeds or premium features. Finished in black, it comes with a simple fabric travel case with a loop enclosure and remains the obvious choice for shoppers focused on the lowest price.

$39.98 at  Walmart										 | 
																$39.98 at  Zagg										 | 
																$49.99 at  Amazon						
					







What’s different about the designs?
All the portable models are designed for travel, folding up neatly to fit into matching compact travel cases. You can arrive at your destination without the usual tangled mess of cables.
The smallest folded Mophie travel charger is the Gen 3, available in the great multi-colored version we’ve tested here and also black if all the fun has drained out of your life. It also features the bi-fold design that takes up less desk space when unfolded. The tri-fold unfolds to a length of nearly a foot across, while the bi-fold measures half that when laid out. That’s because the AirPods charging pad on the bi-fold is hidden behind the more able iPhone adjustable charging stand.

				
					

				
			
Simon Jary




The Roam and Orange/Teal 3-in-1 Travel Charger differ from the Black and Pink versions by hosting the AirPods charging pad behind the orange adjustable iPhone wireless charging stand. This bi-fold design gives it a smaller footprint when opened up, compared to the older models’ longer strip.
The Pink and Black models charge the iPhone only in a flat position, but all three allow the Watch to sit up in Nightstand Mode. The Roam and Orange/Teal models features the stand but can also charge the iPhone flat if you prefer.
The stand for the Roam and Orange chargers is fine for setting the iPhone in a landscape/horizontal StandBy Mode, but less successful with the iPhone is in portrait/vertical when the magnetic placement makes the Watch part lift slightly.

				
					

				
			
Simon Jary



				





How fast can they charge your devices?
The main benefit of the latest Roam travel charger is its more powerful Qi2.2 wireless charging output that means iPhones 16 or later can charge at up to 25W. It beats most other 25W 3-in-1 travel chargers through its StealthCharge technology that protects the phone from the heat generated by such powerful wireless charging by moving the potentially hot components away from the phone charging pad.
Older iPhones  don’t support 25W wireless charging, so remain at Qi2/MagSafe’s 15W maximum. Even then, StealthCharge might make 15W charging a little more efficient, too.

				
					

				
			
Simon Jary




The other Mophie travel chargers are all rated at 15W for all iPhones (12 and later).
While the black Gen 1 charger can reach 5W for fast-charging the Apple Watch, the others support 7.5W charging, which should mean you can put your Watch back on your wrist sooner. The gen 1 charger is also marginally slower powering up compatible AirPods.







How much does each travel charger cost?
Look around as while all the chargers have official retail prices at $149.95, pricing can be cheaper as the products get older—but not always. It would be great to have a mid-ranged product between the premium and super-affordable. It’s likely that the company is selling off the last of the 2021-vintage Gen 1 so stocks will run dry at some stage.
You’ll find the gen 4 Mophie Roam at Apple for $149.95 or £119.95, or buy it direct from Mophie or Zagg UK.
If you are as taken by the Mophie Orange/Teal Special Edition Gen 3 travel charger as I am, it’s still officially priced at $149.95 or £149.95, or check Amazon.
Note that Roam and Orange comes with a 40W wall charger and international plug adapters, while the pink and black travel chargers ship with just a 30W charger, All come with a matching travel case.
Fancy the pretty pink Cherry Blossom Mophie Gen 2 travel charger? Zagg is still selling it as $149.95 or you can find it at Amazon.
If you are after the lowest cost and don’t care for joyful colorways, you can find the Mophie Gen 1 for $39 at Zagg, or $49.95 at Amazon. The cheapest we could find it in the U.K. was £61 at Amazon.
We’ve tested more of the best 3-in-1 iPhone/Watch/AirPods chargers for further comparisons.







Which Mophie 3-in-1 Travel Charger should you buy?
At 25W the Gen 4 Roam is the fastest of all the Mophie travel chargers, although only for iPhones 16 and later. If you aren’t planning on upgrading your iPhone for a while and are happy with 15W charging, consider one of the other models in their fun colors. You may have guessed that the 15W Orange/Teal Gen 3 is a particular favorite—it shares a similar design to the Roam but radically different color scheme, and it’s certainly hard to miss. If you’re more a lover of pink, the Gen 2 Cherry Blossom charger will definitely be for you, but for the cheapest price the original Gen 1 Mophie Travel Charger is hard to beat for budgets.

Here at Macworld we’re extremely fond of Apple’s AirTag, which is a great Bluetooth tracker for an iPhone or Mac user. However, one complaint raised in our AirTag review was that it doesn’t have an attachment (or keyring) hole, which means you’re forced in most situations to buy an accessory to put it in.
Even Apple’s 2026 AirTag hardware update doesn’t change the tracker’s dimensions or lack of attachment hole, so you’ll likely still need one of the great accessories reviewed here.
Want to attach it to your keys? You need to buy a special key ring. Want to attach it to your luggage? Special luggage label. An ecosystem has quickly sprung up offering straps, loops, pet tags, cases and holders for AirTag owners.
UPDATE: The standard AirTag isn’t the only tracker in town that works with Apple’s Find My app. There are now many and varied trackers that work just like an AirTag and sync as items in your Find My app: flat cards, wallets, keychains, glasses cases, passport holders and many more. Check out the best Apple Find My trackers that offer more than even the AIrTag.

If the Apple AirTag is just not right for you, check out these Bluetooth tracker recommended AirTag alternatives.
What you can expect in an AirTag case
Because the AirTag comes in a single variety, you don’t need to choose which kind to acquire. Apple sells them singly ($29) and in a four-pack ($99). Engraving is free.
An AirTag regularly broadcasts 2.4GHz Bluetooth signals with an encrypted device ID for other Apple devices to pick up and relay along with those devices’ locations. The 2.4GHz band penetrates solid objects well, but case designers need to be mindful of materials that have the potential to block the signal. In our survey of AirTag cases, we didn’t find a case so far that had that design problem.
AirTags also use ultrawideband (USB) technology for Precision Finding, exclusive to Apple’s own Find My items. Precision Finding lets an iPhone with UWB identify the direction and distance within inches when it’s within about 15 to 30 feet (4.5 to 9 m).
Consider to what use you may put an AirTag to determine the features you want:
Purpose: Cases exist in enough variety that you can find one designed as a luggage tag, another as a stylish keyring, and another to resist enormous amounts of damage. Figure out where you want to put the AirTag and match the case to it.
Water resistance: Many cases feature some degree of water resistance, some using the IP rating that defines precisely how much. If you’re using an AirTag outside or on a pet’s collar, you may want one with a high degree of resistance. When attaching to a bag or keyring, it may seem less important or not important at all.
Ring, clip, loop, or carabiner: Case makers offer many variants on attachments. Some include a simple hole to attach a keychain, while others incorporate a keychain as part of the product and may include a keyring. You can purchase multiple cases built into a carabiner, including one with a three-digit combination lock. You can also get a string or similar loop design, in which the case passes through a loop and pulls tight on a handle without a knot.
Removable or adhesive: You might want an AirTag case that’s easy to move about or attach and reattach. Other cases include adhesive for semi-permanent fixed attachment.
Hidden for theft recovery: Some cases are designed to hide an AirTag, making its presence less apparent and thus less likely to be discovered if stolen; others are obvious, such as in a keychain or luggage tag. Temper hideability with the knowledge that Apple’s anti-stalking features built into AirTag tech makes them discoverable to criminals with a smartphone.Shows the front: Conversely, some cases show off an AirTag, revealing its front where you might have had added custom engraving from Apple with an emoji or text. You might want to see that engraving to differentiate among AirTags you own.
Cost: Cases generally cost from about $20 to $35—around the price of a single AirTag. However, there are outliers below $10 and above $40. It’s all about the function, ruggedness, and complexity of purpose. Some charge extra for style.
How we test AirTag case features
For each kind of case, we rated them based on specific features around which they were designed. These include:
Easy to insert the AirTag for secure retention: Every case has a slightly different approach to getting an AirTag inside. Some cases have an elaborate locking procedure or require removing and restoring four tiny screws to preserve a waterproof seal. Others are simple as sliding the tag into a holding or popping it into a rubber ring.
Attaches securely for attachable cases: We tested cases that market themselves as attachable at how well they succeed at that task. Cases may come with or be part of a keyring, carabiner, wrist strip, or pet collar, or may have an adhesive to stick on to objects, like the inside of luggage.
Access for battery replacement: Apple expects an AirTag battery to last for about a year in everyday usage, which it defines as one case of Precision Finding and four tones played per day. A case should allow access that isn’t maddening for replacing the battery every several months to a year.
Robust against bumps and bangs: Only a few kinds of cases can avoid the wear and tear of bumping against other objects. Most need to be constructed with that in mind. For cases exposed to other surfaces, we look at whether the materials and build quality give confidence in them provide lasting value.
Blocks access to remove: A handful of cases provide a security element intended to prevent access to an AirTag without excessive force—the AirTag would have to be destroyed to remove it. We rate these cases on whether they seem able to prevent or deter everything but destruction.

title: 10 iPhone Accessibility features that are useful for everyone
content:
Macworld


Apple has always been renowned for adapting its systems to meet the needs of people with disabilities. Anyone who selects Accessibility in the Settings app on an iPhone will be overwhelmed by the sheer range of options available. There are settings for short-sighted people like me, and there are settings for people with age-related vision impairment. There are settings for hearing aids, and a voice can read out the screen content.
As is always the case with Apple’s Accessibility features, there are sliders and buttons tucked away in unexpected places that make life a little easier for all users. Here is a collection of our favorite Accessibility features you could be using.


Face ID attention check

				
					

				
			
Foundry




There’s a rather clever option for Face ID: the biometric module only unlocks the iPhone when you’re looking directly at it. This prevents accidental unlocks. The setting is tucked away in Accessibility under Face ID and Attention.
The system warns you about certain types of sunglasses, but in practice, the unlocking works quite reliably. I’ve never had any problems with my polarized sunglasses. Another useful option is haptic feedback upon successful authentication. You’ll receive a brief vibration when Apple Pay is successful or when the iPhone is unlocked using Face ID.







Notifications with a flash

				
					

				
			
Foundry




You can choose to have notifications on your iPhone signaled visually rather than with an audio alert. This uses the LED flash on the rear camera or a flashing display. The setting can be found under Audio and Visual and is called Flash for Alerts. 
Receiving a large number of notifications can drain the battery more quickly, as the flash or screen is actively switched on.







Always show volume controls

				
					

				
			
Foundry




As part of the Liquid Glass design for iOS 26, Apple removed the volume slider from the widgets. The volume itself could still be controlled via dedicated buttons, gestures on the AirPods, or the Digital Crown on the Apple Watch. The only thing missing was an overview of just how loud AC/DC were rocking or how softly Lana Del Rey was whispering.
However, the slider has never actually disappeared; it can be reactivated in Accessibility under the Audio and Visual section.







No Liquid Glass

				
					

				
			
Foundry




The Liquid Glass interface is here to stay. From the next version of iOS onwards, Apple will no longer accept apps that haven’t yet adapted their appearance to Liquid Glass. However, you can at least make the content stand out better against the background using two settings.
These settings can be found in Accessibility under the Display & Text Size section. The first two sliders after the text settings are called Reduce Transparency and Increase Contrast. Together, these create a clear distinction between the foreground and background, making text easier to read.







On/Off Labels

				
					

				
			
Foundry




If you want to bring a bit of that retro look from previous iOS versions to your iPhone, you can also enable additional On/Off labels in the Display & Text Size section. Instead of relying solely on color cues such as grey and green, the system also provides graphical cues such as a vertical line for On and a circle for Off. These are perhaps the last traces of skeuomorphism in iOS, as the line and circle represent the 0 and 1 in binary code.







Make Siri always aware

				
					

				
			
Foundry




By default, Siri is disabled when the iPhone face down or when the screen is covered. You can change this behavior in Accessibility: go to the Siri section at the end of Accessibility, then turn on Always Listen for Siri. This allows you to activate the smart voice assistant regardless of the iPhone’s position.







Tap on the back

				
					

				
			
Foundry




The Back Tap feature has an interesting history. The Accessibility team at Apple faced a problem with the iPhone X: The Home button disappeared entirely, and with it an intuitive and easy way to take screenshots. Pressing the Volume Up and Power buttons simultaneously requires a fair bit of guitar-playing-like skill, but the team wanted a simple yet effective alternative for people with disabilities.
This is how the double-tap gesture on the back of the iPhone came about as a replacement for the Home button. Initially, it could only be used to take screenshots, but now it offers  several tasks that can be assigned to these taps.
The feature can be found in the Accessibility section, under Touch > Back Tap. You can set up a double-tap and a triple-tap. If you turn on Show Banner, a banner will appear when the iPhone senses a double or triple tap.







Background sounds

				
					

				
			
Foundry




ASMR videos on YouTube attract millions of views: the simple sounds of running water, wind or a crackling fire help people to relax or even fall asleep. Your iPhone can play such sounds too (without ad breaks).
The list of all background sounds can be found in Accessibility under the Audio & Visual section. Under the Background Sound > Sound setting, you’ll find a list of several available options, including Ocean, Rain, Babble, Fire, Airplane, and three different types of white noise. The sounds work even without an internet connection, as the iPhone downloads the relevant soundtrack the first time you play it.
The Background Sound page has several different settings you’ll want to adjust, including Volume, Stop Sounds with a Timer, and more. You can use these background sounds to help you fall asleep and set them to stop at a specific time. 







Reduce frame rate to 60 fps

				
					

				
			
Foundry




On compatible iPhones, you can reduce the refresh rate to 60 frames per second. This is particularly beneficial when using graphically intensive apps. This setting can help reduce heat build-up slightly.. The setting can be found in Accessibility under the Motion section. The setting is at the bottom, called Limit Frame Rate.







One-handed mode

				
					

				
			
Foundry




Having one-handed mode enabled is a must, especially on the larger iPhones. With a downward swipe at the bottom of the screen, all content moves down a little further. Those items become easier to reach. This setting is called Reachability, and the toggle can be found in Accessibility under Touch.

title: Apple Plans iPhone-to-Windows Copy and Paste in EU After Microsoft Request
content:
Apple is working on a new feature that will support cross-device copy and paste between iOS devices and Windows PCs.


Microsoft asked for the feature using Apple's EU interoperability request system for developers, which Apple implemented to comply with the Digital Markets Act. Apple began evaluating the request in March, and on June 26, proposed a project plan. 

Microsoft described how the feature would be used:

 	
Copy text or other supported content on their iPhone and paste it directly on their Windows PC, and vice versa.

 	
Perform common productivity workflows without needing to foreground an app or take explicit repeated actions to initiate a transfer.

 	
Experience clipboard synchronization as a lightweight, continuous capability rather than a manual, app-driven operation.


Apple proposed a solution that would let an iPhone share and import items from the pasteboard to a paired accessory, like a Windows PC. Apple plans to use a solution similar to the Accessory Notifications option it added for third-party wearables in the EU in iOS 26.5. Users would need to give a paired device one-time permission to paste content from an iPhone.
To adopt this solution, you will need to adopt AccessorySetupKit in order for the user to consent to the necessary permissions allowing the pasteboard to be shared with your accessory. This solution will require the user to perform a one-time consent to sharing the pasteboard with each paired accessory that will receive this functionality.

Right now, an app can only read an iPhone's clipboard if the app is actively running in the foreground and the user grants clipboard access with each copy/paste action. For its own devices, Apple has a Universal Clipboard feature with cross-device copy and paste between iOS and macOS.

Microsoft complained that the clipboard restrictions imposed on apps prevent the continuous synchronization of clipboard content from an iPhone to a PC or other connected device in the background. 

Apple says introducing cross-device copy and paste is a significant engineering effort, with work expected to be complete by fall 2027. It will be shipped first in a developer beta for testing ahead of a public release. If the feature is added toward the end of fall 2027, it could be early 2028 before the public gets access.

It is likely that cross-device copy and paste will be limited to iPhone and Windows users in the European Union, though it is possible Apple could implement it worldwide.

Other features, like AirPods-style pairing and notification forwarding for third-party wearables, have only rolled out in the EU.

title: Apple Will Judge Your Mustache Authenticity at Its Ted Lasso Look-Alike Contest
content:
Ted Lasso season four is set to premiere Wednesday, and to celebrate the debut, Apple is hosting a Ted Lasso look-alike contest in New York.


"Think you have the stache to make fans believe? Join the fun this August 6 at Apple Fifth Avenue Plaza for a Ted Lasso Look-Alike contest," reads Apple's Facebook event page. Apple has a set of contest rules instructing participants to visit Apple Fifth Avenue to be judged on "the degree to which they look and act like the character Ted Lasso."

There will be a three-round contest with eliminations in each round. Ten semifinalists will be selected after round one, five finalists will make it past round two, and three finalists will be selected in round three. The event starts at 4:30 p.m. Eastern Time and runs until 7:00 p.m.

 	
Round One, Ted Energy - Contestants have to introduce themselves in character and have a two-minute dance break. Judging will be based on optimism, posture, and presence, along with costume commitment and participation level.

 	
Round Two, Head Coach - Semifinalists will participate in a trivia game and will be judged on the level to which each participant embraces the Ted Lasso character. The round will be judged on trivia results, costume commitment, mustache authenticity (Apple says 'stick-ons OK; real grows extra credit'), and The Believe Factor (something unique and special).

 	
Round Three, Ted Talk - Each remaining contestant will present a 30- to 45-second pep talk to the crowd. It will be judged on how moved the crowd is, costume commitment, and Ted Energy.

Season four of Ted Lasso will premiere on Wednesday, August 5, and it has 10 total episodes. One episode will be released every Wednesday through October 7. title: Fitbit Data Can Finally Sync to Apple Health
content:
The latest update to the Google Health app for iOS allows Google Health data to sync to Apple Health. Google's app is used to collect data from wearables like Fitbit trackers and the Pixel Watch.


Sync to Apple Health. Share your data like your exercise records, sleep, vitals, steps, and more from Google Health to Apple Health.

Google Health (previously the Fitbit app) collects fitness, sleep, and wellness data from a connected wearable device. Steps, distance traveled, heart rate, sleep, and more can now be added to Apple Health. As noted on Reddit, some data such as HRV doesn't transfer over.

Syncing can be enabled after downloading the update by selecting Connections, choosing Apps and services, and then adding Apple Health.

Apple Health data already synced to Google Health, so the new update adds two-way sync between the platforms. Fitbit devices have never had native sync to Apple Health, and users previously had to use a third-party syncing utility or a workaround to transfer data.

available from the App Store for free. The update also adds Smart Health Links for sharing medical records with providers or family members.
